title: ⭐⭐ Practice: whose words, and what the change of moment does to them

questions.prompt: On Friday, standing in the computer room, the technician said to the club: "I am testing the new router here today." On Monday, from the office at the other end of the school, Emna reports those words to a friend. Leaving the verb and the pronoun aside, which words of the technician's sentence can no longer be kept as they are, and why?

options.text: "here" only, because the sentence does not name a day.
"today" only, because a word of place is never touched in a report.
Neither of them: the words a person actually used must be kept exactly as they were said.
"here" and "today", because Emna is neither in that room nor on that day.

questions.explanation: The line naming "here" and "today", because Emna is neither in that room nor on that day, is right: here points at the place of the person speaking and today at the day she speaks, so once the report is made in another room and three days later, both words point at the wrong place and the wrong moment. They become there and that day. The line naming "here" only, because the sentence does not name a day, forgets that today names a day just as surely as Friday would. The line naming "today" only, because a word of place is never touched in a report, states a rule that does not exist: here changes for exactly the same reason as today. And "Neither of them: the words a person actually used must be kept exactly as they were said." describes direct speech, where inverted commas do keep the exact words; a report has no inverted commas, and its job is to keep the sense true from where you now stand.

questions.prompt: A report on a school computer room says: "The machines are getting less and less reliable." Which of these four facts does that sentence record?

options.text: They break down more often than before, and the change is not over.
They have never been reliable at any moment of their life.
They broke down once, and that once was very bad.
They are less reliable than the machines of the school on the other side of town.

questions.explanation: "They break down more often than before, and the change is not over." is right: two comparatives joined by and record a movement that is under way and still going, and less and less points that movement downwards. "They have never been reliable at any moment of their life." denies that anything changed at all, whereas the sentence is entirely about a change. "They broke down once, and that once was very bad." replaces a movement with a single event; a doubled comparative can never describe one occasion. And "They are less reliable than the machines of the school on the other side of town." is what a plain comparative does, comparing two things at one moment; the doubled comparative compares the machines with themselves, earlier.

questions.prompt: At Tuesday's meeting Hedi said: "I bought this microphone for the radio club." A fortnight later the secretary writes up the minutes, far from the meeting room: "Hedi said that he had bought ___ microphone for the radio club." Which word fills the gap?

options.text: this
these
the
a

questions.explanation: "the" is right: this and these placed in front of a noun point at an object the speaker can show, and once the report is written elsewhere there is nothing to point at, so the demonstrative gives way to the definite article. "this" keeps the pointing word in a sentence where nobody can follow the finger; it belongs in the inverted commas Hedi used, not in the minutes. "these" adds a second fault to the first, since microphone is singular and these is plural. And "a" would present the microphone as a new thing the reader has never heard of, when the whole point of the minutes is that it is the one Hedi bought.

questions.prompt: A science page for young readers ends on this line: "Nothing in the survey proves it, so the two researchers ___ that most families will own one screen for each child." Which word of the lesson fills the gap?

options.text: survive
assume
conceal
relieve

questions.explanation: "assume" is right: to assume is to take something as true when you have not proved it, and the first half of the sentence, nothing in the survey proves it, sets up exactly that situation. "survive" means to stay alive, or to come through a difficulty without being destroyed, and no difficulty is being come through here. "conceal" means to hide something on purpose so that others do not learn it; the researchers are publishing their idea, not hiding it. And "relieve" means to take away a pain or a worry, which is something you do to a person, not to a statement about the future.

questions.prompt: A school magazine prints this line about a visitor: "The engineer told the pupils that she had learned to code on a machine older than they were." Which of these four sentences is the one she actually said?

options.text: "I had learned to code on a machine older than you were."
"She learned to code on a machine older than they were."
"I learn to code on a machine older than you are."
"I learned to code on a machine older than you are."

questions.explanation: The sentence "I learned to code on a machine older than you are." is the one she said: you undo every change, one by one. The engineer speaking of herself says I, and speaking to the pupils in front of her says you; had learned is where a past simple lands once the report is made in the past, so it goes back to learned; and the were of the comparison goes back to are, since it too had stepped back. The sentence "I had learned to code on a machine older than you were." keeps the report's own tenses inside the inverted commas, where they never belonged. The sentence "She learned to code on a machine older than they were." leaves the third person in place, so the engineer would be speaking about somebody else. And the sentence "I learn to code on a machine older than you are." puts the verb in the simple present, which had learned cannot come from: a simple present becomes a simple past in a report, and never goes further back than that.

questions.prompt: In the class debate on time spent online, Mouna says: "Anyone who spends five hours a night on the net has stopped living." Wassim thinks the hours are worth discussing but that the end of her sentence goes far too far, and he does not want to throw away everything she said. Which reply does exactly that?

options.text: You are right about the hours, but the last three words go much too far.
That is exactly it, and nobody in this room could argue with a word of it.
You are completely wrong, and everybody in this room knows that you are.
I would rather not take a side on that question at all.

questions.explanation: "You are right about the hours, but the last three words go much too far." is right: it keeps what is defensible in Mouna's sentence, the number of hours, and refuses only what is excessive, has stopped living. That double move, agreeing in part and then marking the limit, is what disagreeing properly looks like in a debate. "That is exactly it, and nobody in this room could argue with a word of it." agrees with the whole of it, including the part Wassim rejects. "You are completely wrong, and everybody in this room knows that you are." throws away the hours along with the rest and answers with a crowd instead of an argument. And "I would rather not take a side on that question at all." is a refusal to speak: Wassim has an opinion, and this sentence hides it.
